items.anchor_quote: Research Questions and Challenges for Improved Spacecraft Fire Detection
items.summary: Exact document title: 'Research Questions and Challenges for Improved Spacecraft Fire Detection'.
items.scope_notes: Bibliographic. No printed page numbers anywhere in the PDF, so printed_page is null for all items.

items.anchor_quote: A topical white paper submitted to the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering and
items.summary: The cover identifies the document as a topical white paper submitted to the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering and Medicine (NASEM) for the Biological and Physical Sciences Decadal Survey; the cover labels the survey '2022-2032'. No date is printed in the document body; the PDF metadata creation date is 2021-10-31 and the file name ends in 211031.
items.scope_notes: The cover label '2022-2032' differs from the label '2023-2032' that the same paper uses for the same decadal survey in its reference 41 (pdf page 10). The date comes from PDF metadata/file name, not from printed text.

items.anchor_quote: Claire Fortenberry Universities Space Research Association, NASA Glenn Research Center
items.summary: Primary author: Claire Fortenberry, Universities Space Research Association (USRA) at NASA Glenn Research Center (contact details for GRC are printed on the cover).

items.anchor_quote: Xiaoliang Wang, Desert Research Institute
items.summary: Coauthors: Xiaoliang Wang (Desert Research Institute); Thomas Cleary (NIST); John Easton (Case Western Reserve University, NASA GRC); Gordon Berger (USRA, NASA GRC); Marit Meyer (NASA GRC).

items.anchor_quote: Luca Carmignani, University of California, Berkeley; Daniel Dietrich, NASA Glenn Research
items.summary: 23 cosigners are listed: Luca Carmignani (UC Berkeley); Daniel Dietrich (NASA GRC); Christian Eigenbrod (ZARM, University of Bremen, Germany); A. Carlos Fernandez-Pello (UC Berkeley); Osamu Fujita (Hokkaido University, Japan); Michael Gollner (UC Berkeley); Augustin Guibaud (University College London, UK); Michael Johnston (USRA, NASA GRC); Grunde Jomaas (FRISSBE, Slovenian National Building and Civil Engineering Institute (ZAG), Slovenia); Sarah Kingsley (Georgia Institute of Technology); Guillaume Legros (CNRS, France); Ya-Ting Liao (Case Western Reserve University); Randall McDermott (NIST); Fletcher Miller (San Diego State University); Justin Niehaus (NASA GRC); Thomas Orlando (Georgia Institute of Technology); Rosa Padilla (USRA, NASA GRC); Gary Ruff (NASA GRC); Nickolay Smirnov (Moscow Lomonosov State University, Russia); Benjamin Sumlin (USRA, NASA GRC); James T'ien (Case Western Reserve University); David Urban (NASA GRC); Indrek Wichman (Michigan State University).
items.scope_notes: Cosigners are distinct from authors; the paper is a multi-institution white paper led from NASA GRC, not a NASA technical report.

items.anchor_quote: This paper describes challenges and recommendations for research to improve spacecraft fire detection.
items.summary: Stated purpose: to set out challenges and research recommendations for improving spacecraft fire detection, motivated by crew safety and the need for detectors that catch a wide variety of fires.

items.anchor_quote: Fire emissions are affected by fuel type, heating conditions, gravity and exploration atmosphere.
items.summary: The abstract names four factors that affect fire emissions: fuel type, heating conditions, gravity, and the exploration (cabin) atmosphere.
items.scope_notes: Framing statement; no data attached at this point.

items.anchor_quote: Advances in sensing technology provide a promising basis for future detectors, which must
items.summary: The abstract says sensing-technology advances are a promising basis for future detectors, which must be able to selectively detect a broad variety of fires; addressing these areas is presented as key to future lunar and deep-space missions.

items.anchor_quote: refers specifically to the heat and radiation produced from the reaction of
items.summary: Definition used: 'fire' means the heat and radiation from a flammable material reacting with oxygen.

items.anchor_quote: fire detection must also encompass the period of fuel overheating prior to flame development
items.summary: Because early detection is preferred, the authors state that fire detection in practice must also cover the fuel-overheating phase before any flame develops.
items.scope_notes: Sets detection scope to include pre-flame overheating (oxidative pyrolysis), not only flaming fires.

items.anchor_quote: spacecraft fires are especially dangerous due to limited escape options and extinguishment resources
items.summary: Compared with building fires on Earth, spacecraft fires are described as especially dangerous because of limited escape and extinguishing resources; even a survivable fire releases toxic particles and gases that threaten crew health.

items.anchor_quote: Detectable properties of fire include heat, radiation, and smoke.
items.summary: Detectable fire properties are heat, radiation and smoke. 'Smoke' is defined to include gases (examples given: CO, CO2, water vapour, volatile organics) and particles formed either by overheating the fuel (oxidative pyrolysis) or by a flame (e.g., soot and ash).

items.anchor_quote: In microgravity, this buoyant flow does not occur, and this advantage therefore does not exist.
items.summary: On Earth smoke detection is advantageous because buoyancy carries hot combustion products upward, so ceiling-mounted detectors sit where smoke concentrates (heat and radiation detectors are noted as useful for select terrestrial applications, ref. 1). In microgravity there is no buoyant flow, so this placement advantage is lost.
items.scope_notes: Physical argument about smoke transport and detector placement; no test data given here.

items.anchor_quote: smoke detectors are placed in the cabin air return vents in front of the filters
items.summary: As a consequence of the lack of buoyant flow, ISS smoke detectors are located in the cabin air return vents, upstream of the filters; the authors note this placement has further implications for fire detection that they discuss later in the paper.
items.scope_notes: Describes ISS detector siting. The later discussion (same page) concerns ECLSS filtration outpacing smoke accumulation (ref. 6).

items.anchor_quote: Due to a lack of data characterizing microgravity fires, however, spacecraft fire detection
items.summary: Because data characterising microgravity fires were lacking, spacecraft fire detection strategies have had to rely on technology developed for terrestrial fire detection.

items.anchor_quote: the ionization detector on the Space Shuttle represented the most advanced detection technology
items.summary: Historical example: the Space Shuttle ionization detector reflected the most advanced detection technology of the 1970s, when ionization detectors were spreading in homes.
items.detector: ionization detector on the Space Shuttle

items.anchor_quote: the ISS forward light scattering detector utilized improvements in photodiode technology developed
items.summary: Similarly, the ISS forward light scattering detector drew on 1990s improvements in photodiode technology (ref. 2).
items.scope_notes: Identifies the ISS smoke detector type as forward light scattering.

items.anchor_quote: Recent research has demonstrated that current fire detection strategies are inadequate for ensuring
items.summary: The authors state that recent research has shown current fire detection strategies to be inadequate for ensuring crew safety on long-duration missions; the following sentences give the supporting evidence (SAME missed alarms, ECLSS filtration, dust nuisance alarms).
items.scope_notes: Authors' summary judgement, not a single measured result.

items.anchor_quote: which was the first study to examine oxidative pyrolysis particles in microgravity
items.summary: The Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME) is described as the first study to examine oxidative pyrolysis (overheating) smoke particles in microgravity.
items.scope_notes: Only SAME is named; SAME-R (the reflight) is not mentioned anywhere in this white paper.

items.anchor_quote: the ISS detector failed to alarm for Kapton smoke in half of the tests
items.summary: In SAME, the ISS detector did not alarm for Kapton smoke in half of the tests. Refs. 3-5 are cited for the SAME results: Meyer et al. 2015 (Aerosol Sci. Technol. 49(5):299-309, moment method), Mulholland et al. 2015 (Aerosol Sci. Technol. 49(5):310-321, low-gravity pyrolysis smoke), and Meyer et al. 2018 (Fire Saf. J. 98:74-81, spacecraft smoke detector performance in low gravity).

numbers.meaning: share of SAME Kapton smoke tests in which the ISS detector failed to alarm (50 is a conversion of the printed word 'half')

items.scope_notes: Missed alarm (no alarm while smoke was present), not a false alarm. The white paper gives no test count, no heating temperature, aging time, flow speed or alarm threshold, and does not say which of refs. 3-5 holds the figure. 'ISS detector' here is, per the same page, the ISS forward light scattering detector. Applies to SAME only; SAME-R is not mentioned. Wording 'half' is as printed; the task brief's 'roughly 50%' is not the source wording.

items.anchor_quote: and for Teflon smoke in two-thirds of the tests, a troubling result
items.summary: In the same SAME sentence, the ISS detector did not alarm for Teflon smoke in two-thirds of the tests (same citations, refs. 3-5).

numbers.meaning: share of SAME Teflon smoke tests in which the ISS detector failed to alarm (66.7 is a rounded conversion of the printed 'two-thirds')

items.scope_notes: Missed alarm, not false alarm. No test count or test conditions are given in the white paper; the denominator must be taken from refs. 3-5. Applies to SAME only (SAME-R not mentioned). The task brief's 'roughly 67%' is a conversion; printed wording is 'two-thirds'.

items.anchor_quote: Kapton and Teflon are abundant in spacecraft electrical systems, where a spacecraft fire is likely
items.summary: The authors call the SAME missed-alarm result troubling because Kapton and Teflon are abundant in spacecraft electrical systems, where a spacecraft fire is likely to begin (refs. 3-5 cited at sentence end).

items.anchor_quote: particle filtration rates provided by the Environmental Control and Life Support System (ECLSS)
items.summary: Urban et al. (2016, ref. 6) are cited as showing that ECLSS particle filtration is fast enough to outpace smoke accumulation for a small or early-stage fire, so detection may fail or be delayed if the event does not raise cabin smoke concentration to the detector's alarm threshold.
items.scope_notes: Concerns small/early-stage fires and the detector alarm threshold (detector not further specified in this sentence). The white paper does not state whether ref. 6 is an analysis/model or an experiment, nor give filtration rates or thresholds. 'May fail or be delayed' is a hedged implication, not a counted missed alarm.

items.anchor_quote: because the ISS detector does not select for smoke particles, the device is
items.summary: Because the ISS detector is not selective for smoke particles, it is prone to nuisance alarms from suspended dust, which can desensitise the crew to real alarms.
items.scope_notes: False/nuisance alarm (alarm without fire, from dust). No alarm counts or rates are given; no citation is attached to this sentence.

items.anchor_quote: when ISS crew members vacuum the cabin, they typically disable the smoke
items.summary: Operational practice reported: when ISS crew vacuum the cabin they typically disable the smoke detectors so that suspended dust does not trigger alarms.
items.scope_notes: Operational workaround for dust nuisance alarms; the paper gives no frequency, duration or citation. It does not quantify the time detectors are disabled.

items.anchor_quote: relying on detection of a single fire property, like the forward light scattering
items.summary: From these observations the authors conclude that a system relying on a single fire property, such as the ISS forward light scattering detector, is unlikely to achieve successful early fire detection in all relevant scenarios.
items.detector: forward light scattering detector on the ISS
items.scope_notes: Authors' inference from SAME missed alarms, filtration analysis and dust nuisance alarms; motivates the multi-sensor recommendation (Section D, Recommendation 4).

items.anchor_quote: future experiments must address the shortcomings of traditional fire detection methods and establish
items.summary: Future experiments must address shortcomings of traditional fire detection methods and establish optimal detection methods for future spacecraft.

items.anchor_quote: as missions move deeper into space and utilize different exploration atmospheres, new risks
items.summary: As missions go deeper into space and use different exploration atmospheres, new risks arise that must be evaluated.

items.anchor_quote: flammability limits are not expected to meet current requirements under elevated O2 (34%) and
items.summary: Material flammability limits are not expected to meet current requirements under the elevated-oxygen (34%) and reduced-pressure (8.2 psi) conditions planned for future lunar habitats; these conditions are also expected to affect fire emissions.
items.scope_notes: Expectation for planned conditions, not a measurement. pressure_kpa converted from 8.2 psi (x6.894757); printed value is in psi.

items.location: Introduction, end of para 3 (sentence starts on pdf page 2)
items.anchor_quote: realistic fire scenarios, characterization of gravity and exploration impacts on fire signatures, and
items.summary: Research topics to investigate: identifying realistic fire scenarios; characterising how gravity and exploration atmospheres affect fire signatures; and developing novel detectors that selectively detect a wider range of spacecraft fires.

items.anchor_quote: Identification of realistic fire scenarios and characterization of fire signatures from
items.summary: Topic A: identify realistic fire scenarios and characterise fire signatures of unstudied and understudied fuels; since a detection system must catch smoke from many scenarios, the fuels of interest must be identified and examined thoroughly.

items.anchor_quote: Experiments should examine both small scale (similar to SAME) and large-scale fires
items.summary: Experiments should cover both small-scale fires (like SAME) and large-scale fires (like the Saffire experiments, refs. 7-9), to evaluate detection of early-stage and fully developed spacecraft fires respectively.
items.scope_notes: Only mention of Saffire in the body text; no Saffire results are reported in the white paper.

items.anchor_quote: A fire source of major concern is the lithium ion battery
items.summary: Lithium ion batteries (LIBs) are a major fire-source concern; they power on-orbit laptops, power tools and space suits.

items.anchor_quote: laptop LIB fires constitute one of the most likely and most dangerous spacecraft fire
items.summary: Laptop LIB fires are described as among the most likely and most dangerous spacecraft fire scenarios for long-duration missions (ref. 10).

items.anchor_quote: increased reliance on LIBs to power electrical components for longer periods of time
items.summary: The community anticipates more reliance on LIBs, for longer periods, as crewed missions move to the Moon, Mars and beyond (ref. 11).

items.anchor_quote: we are aware of only one study that characterized the properties of smoke
items.summary: Gap: several studies have examined gaseous products of LIB fires (refs. 12-15) and particles from large-scale LIB fires such as car batteries (refs. 16-17), but the authors know of only one study (ref. 18) characterising smoke particles from laptop LIB fires.
items.scope_notes: Gap as of the authors' 2021 awareness; not a claim that no other study exists.

items.anchor_quote: Another fuel of immediate interest is the to-be-determined fabric that will compose crew
items.summary: A second fuel of immediate interest is the not-yet-selected fabric for crew clothing in future lunar missions.

items.anchor_quote: clothing worn by crew members on the ISS (e.g., cotton jersey t-shirts) may not be
items.summary: Because planned exploration atmospheres are expected to raise material flammability, ISS crew clothing (e.g., cotton jersey t-shirts) may be unsuitable for lunar missions; a fire-resistant fabric is being sought for the lunar habitat.
items.scope_notes: Expectation; no flammability data given here.

items.anchor_quote: This fabric must be investigated as a potential fuel to identify fire signatures
items.summary: The chosen fabric must be tested as a potential fuel to identify its fire signatures, which will guide selection of an optimal fire detector.

items.anchor_quote: the same fuel heated to different maximum temperatures can yield particles with
items.summary: Differences in heating method complicate scenario definition: ground experiments in Meyer (2015, ref. 19) showed that one fuel heated to different maximum temperatures can give particles of drastically different sizes and morphologies.
items.scope_notes: Ground experiments; the white paper does not name the fuels or temperatures here.

items.anchor_quote: the longer fuel residence time experienced in reduced gravity drastically impact the formation and growth
items.summary: Parabolic-flight measurements show that longer fuel residence time in reduced gravity strongly affects particle formation and growth (ref. 20), fundamentally changing how readily a flame produces smoke from a given fuel (ref. 21).
items.scope_notes: Refs. 20-21 (Guibaud et al. 2020) concern flames spreading over polyethylene-coated wires in opposed flow, per their titles; applies to flaming smoke, not oxidative pyrolysis.

items.anchor_quote: Future spacecraft smoke detection studies must attempt to recreate a variety of realistic overheating
items.summary: Future spacecraft smoke detection studies should reproduce a range of realistic overheating scenarios, including different peak heating temperatures and different temperature ramp methods.

items.anchor_quote: most spacecraft detection research to date has focused on characterization of smoke sizes
items.summary: Because recent spacecraft detectors sense smoke particles, most spacecraft detection research so far has concentrated on smoke particle sizes and morphologies.

items.anchor_quote: there is a need for expanded smoke measurements including but not limited to gas
items.summary: Owing to challenges with particle detection, smoke measurements need to be expanded to include, among others, gas composition and concentrations, particle charge distributions and particle chemical composition.

items.anchor_quote: monomers generated from polymer degradation during a fire constitute a potential detection target
items.summary: Extra flammable gases released in microgravity fires can feed flame propagation (example: vapour jetting of monomers in PMMA combustion, ref. 22), so monomers from polymer degradation are a potential gas-phase detection target.

items.anchor_quote: potential gas-phase detection targets are electrolyte vapors vented in the early stages of LIB
items.summary: Electrolyte vapours vented early in LIB failure are another candidate gas-phase detection target.
items.scope_notes: Proposed target; no detection data in the white paper.

items.anchor_quote: Ground measurements of particles and gases from spacecraft-relevant sources could inform future
items.summary: Characterising spacecraft-relevant fire signatures would also benefit Earth: ground measurements could inform terrestrial smoke detector standards and, for LIBs (laptops, phones, electric vehicles), help evaluate detection standards and air-quality risks from LIB fires.

items.anchor_quote: Evaluation of gravity impacts on fire signatures and plume transport.
items.summary: Topic B: evaluate how gravity affects fire signatures and smoke plume transport.

items.anchor_quote: spacecraft fire detection studies have focused on microgravity applications, with heavy reliance on
items.summary: So far, spacecraft fire detection studies have targeted microgravity and leaned heavily on complementary ground experiments.
items.scope_notes: Implies partial gravity (lunar/Martian) is comparatively unstudied within this source's framing.

items.anchor_quote: smoke particles generated in microgravity were larger compared to those generated in ground experiments
items.summary: In SAME, smoke particles produced in microgravity were larger than those from ground experiments below an air-flow threshold of 8.1 cm/s, with the largest size and morphology differences seen in no-flow tests.

numbers.meaning: air-flow threshold below which microgravity particles were larger than ground particles

items.scope_notes: airflow_cm_s left null because 8.1 cm/s is a threshold (below it), not a single test condition. Materials and test counts not stated in the white paper.

items.anchor_quote: Differences in particle formation and evolution in reduced gravity are attributable to increased residence
items.summary: The authors attribute the reduced-gravity particle differences to longer residence times near the smoke source, because plumes disperse slowly at low air speeds without buoyant flow (refs. 3, 4).

items.anchor_quote: In lunar gravity, the dependence of smoke particle size on air flow remains unclear.
items.summary: Open question: how smoke particle size depends on air flow in lunar gravity is not known.

items.anchor_quote: particle sizes must be characterized in reduced gravity under air velocity conditions relevant
items.summary: To choose a suitable detector for a lunar habitat, particle sizes must be measured in reduced gravity at air velocities relevant to that environment.

items.anchor_quote: Experiments must also examine particle growth over relevant timescales
items.summary: Experiments must also track particle growth over relevant timescales, chosen using cabin air transport parameters and space-specific environmental conditions.

items.anchor_quote: the effects of reduced gravity on smoke particle properties should be examined for a
items.summary: Reduced-gravity effects on smoke particle properties should be studied across a variety of spacecraft-relevant fuels.

items.anchor_quote: The magnitude of gravity influences smoke plume
items.summary: Gravity level affects smoke plume transport, illustrated by Figure 1, which compares plume transport in terrestrial, microgravity and lunar gravity (per the caption).
items.scope_notes: Only the caption text was extracted; the figure graphic was not analysed.

items.anchor_quote: The optimal location for a smoke detector within a lunar vehicle cabin must be
items.summary: Where to put a smoke detector in a lunar vehicle cabin must be determined by further research.

items.anchor_quote: Lunar dust is expected to pose a significant threat to crew health and
items.summary: Lunar dust is expected to threaten crew health and materials; floor-level air returns would help remove lunar dust from cabin air via gravitational settling.
items.scope_notes: Expectation; relevant to dust nuisance alarms and to detector siting near returns.

items.anchor_quote: it may be advantageous to place detectors on the cabin ceilings
items.summary: If buoyant transport in lunar gravity is strong enough to overcome the downward (floor-return) flow, ceiling-mounted detectors may be advantageous.
items.scope_notes: Conditional and hedged ('may'); no modelling or test result given.

items.anchor_quote: Modeling smoke transport in lunar gravity is therefore prioritized for upcoming fire safety research.
items.summary: Modelling smoke transport in lunar gravity is therefore made a priority for upcoming fire safety research.

items.anchor_quote: the development of a lunar gravity smoke model could provide the framework for Martian studies
items.summary: A lunar-gravity smoke model could later serve as the framework for Mars studies.

items.anchor_quote: smoke emission factors (i.e., mass of smoke component per mass fuel burned)
items.summary: Future fire safety modelling will depend on smoke emission factors, defined as mass of a smoke component per mass of fuel burned, measured in microgravity and partial-gravity experiments (ref. 6).

items.anchor_quote: determination of realistic emission factors for different fuels and fire scenarios are critical for
items.summary: Emission factors combined with habitat filtration and mixing parameters allow alarm-time predictions; because cabin air is usually well mixed and heavily filtered, realistic emission factors for different fuels and scenarios are critical for predicting time to alarm and for choosing detector placement.
items.scope_notes: Detection time is discussed only as a prediction need; no alarm times are reported in the paper.

items.anchor_quote: Evaluation of exploration atmosphere impacts on fire signatures in reduced gravity.
items.summary: Topic C: evaluate how exploration atmospheres affect fire signatures in reduced gravity.

items.anchor_quote: planned environment for future lunar habitats is 34% O2 and 8.2 psi
items.summary: The planned lunar habitat atmosphere is 34% O2 at 8.2 psi (ref. 23).
items.scope_notes: Planned condition, not a tested one. pressure_kpa converted from psi.

items.anchor_quote: expected to influence material flammability, flame spread rates, and smoke emission for materials
items.summary: These atmosphere parameters together with reduced gravity are expected to influence material flammability, flame spread rates and smoke emission (refs. 21, 24-26).
items.scope_notes: Expectation; no detector data.

items.anchor_quote: methane flames, soot surface growth and oxidation rates increase as O2 % increases
items.summary: Lee et al. (2000, ref. 27) found that in methane flames soot surface growth and oxidation rates rise with oxygen percentage.
items.scope_notes: Terrestrial laboratory flame study with a gaseous fuel; not a spacecraft detection test.

items.anchor_quote: soot inception and surface growth rates increase by orders of magnitude, with substantial changes
items.summary: Edland et al. (2020, ref. 28) showed that in propane flames soot inception and surface growth rates rise by orders of magnitude, with large changes above 30% O2.

numbers.meaning: oxygen level above which substantial soot changes occurred

items.scope_notes: Gaseous fuel, technical-scale turbulent flames on Earth; not a detection test.

items.anchor_quote: below a critical pressure at which soot formation is maximized, reduced pressures are expected
items.summary: Below the critical pressure at which soot formation peaks, lower pressures are expected to reduce soot formation (ref. 29).
items.scope_notes: Critical pressure value not given in the white paper.

items.location: Section C (sentence continues on pdf page 5)
items.anchor_quote: pressure conditions targeted for future lunar vehicles are expected to impact sizes, and therefore
items.summary: Based on these studies, the elevated O2 and reduced pressure targeted for lunar vehicles are expected to change soot sizes from fully developed fires, and therefore their detection.
items.scope_notes: Expectation inferred from gaseous-fuel flame studies (refs. 27-29); not a measured detection result. Applies to soot from fully developed (flaming) fires.

items.anchor_quote: these studies utilized gaseous fuels rather than solid fuels, and more research is needed
items.summary: The cited soot studies used gaseous fuels; more research is needed on how O2 and pressure affect solid fuel combustion.

items.anchor_quote: Effects of O2 concentration and pressure on oxidative pyrolysis particles remain unclear
items.summary: How O2 concentration and pressure affect oxidative pyrolysis (overheating) particles is unclear and must be investigated.

items.anchor_quote: Development of improved fire detection systems.
items.summary: Topic D: develop improved fire detection systems, using experiments that characterise fire signatures under spacecraft-relevant conditions as the basis.

items.anchor_quote: a CO detector in parallel with a smoke detector was suggested as a solution
items.summary: Urban et al. (2016, ref. 6) suggested pairing a CO detector with a smoke detector to counter rapid particle filtration by the ECLSS.
items.detector: CO detector in parallel with a smoke detector
items.scope_notes: Proposal from ref. 6; the white paper reports no test of this configuration.

items.anchor_quote: an ideal spacecraft fire detection system would incorporate a network of instruments and sensors
items.summary: An ideal spacecraft fire detection system would use a network of instruments and sensors monitoring fire properties in the cabin: temperature, radiation, gas composition and concentrations, and particle properties and concentrations.
items.scope_notes: Multi-property / multi-sensor concept; stated as an ideal, not a demonstrated system.

items.anchor_quote: The feasibility of such a system must be addressed in future work.
items.summary: Whether such a networked system is feasible must be addressed in future work.

items.anchor_quote: utilize monitoring technology already incorporated into the spacecraft for other purposes, like cabin air
items.summary: A sensor network for fire detection could reuse monitoring technology already on the spacecraft for other purposes, such as cabin air quality monitoring.

items.anchor_quote: gas monitors currently on the ISS, including a laser spectroscopy-based combustion products
items.summary: ISS gas monitors, including a laser spectroscopy-based combustion products monitor (ref. 30), could be folded into a larger fire detection network in a future vehicle.

items.anchor_quote: only expand the subset of detectable fires but would also reduce false alarms
items.summary: An array of sensors continuously watching for predetermined fire signatures would both widen the set of detectable fires and reduce false alarms.
items.scope_notes: Expected benefit; no false-alarm rates are reported.

items.anchor_quote: measuring particle chemical composition or charges could differentiate between smoke particles and lunar dust
items.summary: A future detector that measures particle chemical composition or charge could distinguish smoke particles from lunar dust, greatly improving fire safety in lunar spacecraft.
items.scope_notes: Proposed discrimination approach against dust false alarms; not demonstrated in the paper.

items.anchor_quote: have enabled in situ molecular-level particle and gas chemical characterization
items.summary: Advances in chemical measurement (e.g., gas chromatography mass spectrometry) allow in situ molecular-level characterisation of particles and gases; work to shorten analysis time, cut power and footprint and improve robustness (refs. 31-33) makes these candidates for selective smoke detectors.

items.anchor_quote: Chemical characterization of particles and gases produced during a fire can also provide
items.summary: Chemical characterisation of fire particles and gases could also reveal what material is burning, the approximate fire temperature and the toxicity of products; immediate knowledge of these would help choose the best fire response (ref. 34).

items.anchor_quote: machine learning techniques like positive matrix factorization
items.summary: Novel data analysis, including positive matrix factorization (refs. 35-37) and deep long short-term memory networks with variational autoencoders (ref. 38), could reduce complex data sets and identify analyte sources efficiently.

items.anchor_quote: Table 1 lists a subset of resources currently available for spacecraft smoke characterization
items.summary: The Capabilities section introduces Table 1 as a partial list of resources available for spacecraft smoke characterisation research.

items.anchor_quote: Gases and Aerosols from Smoldering Polymers (GASP)
items.summary: At NASA GRC, the Gases and Aerosols from Smoldering Polymers (GASP) laboratory (ref. 19) and the new Battery Test Facility (BTF) support ground testing at terrestrial O2 and pressure.

items.anchor_quote: Parabolic flights provide short durations of microgravity or partial gravity (approximately 30 s)
items.summary: Parabolic flights give short periods (approximately 30 s) of microgravity or partial gravity, useful to prove experiment feasibility before longer missions (refs. 20, 21, 39).

numbers.meaning: approximate duration of reduced gravity per parabola

items.anchor_quote: drop tower centrifuge rig can currently provide 5.2 seconds of lunar gravity
items.summary: The Zero-Gravity Research Facility (ZGRF) drop tower centrifuge rig currently provides 5.2 s of lunar gravity (ref. 40); planned GRC drop tower upgrades would extend reduced-gravity time to 10 s (ref. 41).

numbers.meaning: current lunar-gravity duration of ZGRF centrifuge rig
planned reduced-gravity duration after drop tower improvements

items.anchor_quote: Experiments on lunar vehicles (e.g., through Commercial Lunar Payload Services) are necessary
items.summary: Experiments on lunar vehicles (e.g., via Commercial Lunar Payload Services) are needed to thoroughly study the effect of partial gravity on fire emissions.

items.anchor_quote: continued combustion experiments on the ISS (e.g., using the microgravity science glovebox
items.summary: Continued ISS combustion experiments (e.g., Microgravity Science Glovebox, refs. 42-43; Combustion Integrated Rack, ref. 44) and future low-Earth-orbit spacecraft are needed to improve microgravity fire detection, which stays relevant for deep-space missions.

items.anchor_quote: improvements in sensing technology for both particles and gases will enable unprecedented measurements
items.summary: Better particle and gas sensing technology will allow unprecedented measurements within spacecraft constraints.

items.anchor_quote: sensors can be calibrated to reference aerosols and instruments to provide particle size distributions
items.summary: Beyond instruments already used on spacecraft (refs. 30, 45), novel sensors can be calibrated against reference aerosols and instruments to give particle size distributions and concentrations (refs. 46-47).
items.scope_notes: Refs. 46-47 evaluate low-cost particulate sensors on Earth (per titles).

items.anchor_quote: Particle and gas sensors increasingly feature smaller footprints and power requirements
items.summary: Particle and gas sensors are getting smaller and lower-power, a logistical advantage for future lunar and deep-space chamber studies.

items.anchor_quote: is crucial for determining detector design and placement strategies
items.summary: Using computational fluid dynamics to assess whether fire effluent can be detected as it spreads from the source is crucial for detector design and placement strategies.

items.anchor_quote: designed for fire flows in any gravity environment with fire or other heat sources
items.summary: The NIST Fire Dynamics Simulator (FDS) is cited as a model built for fire flows in any gravity environment (refs. 48-49).

items.anchor_quote: Recent updates to FDS include advancements in aerosol dynamics modeling
items.summary: Recent FDS updates add aerosol dynamics, tracking particle size distributions and processes that change particle size and concentration (coagulation, deposition, thermophoresis).

items.anchor_quote: the code may be modified to account for currently un-modeled physics
items.summary: Because FDS is free and open source, it can be modified to include physics it does not yet model.
items.scope_notes: The paper does not list which physics are un-modelled.

items.anchor_quote: Partial list of experimental resources enabling investigation of smoke particle
items.summary: Table 1 is a partial list of experimental resources for studying smoke particle characteristics and transport under various gravity and cabin atmosphere conditions; columns are duration, gravity (g), O2 (%) and pressure (psi).

items.anchor_quote: GASP and BTF (GRC) Full burn 1 21 14.7

items.anchor_quote: Transformative spacecraft fire detection research is paramount to ensuring crew safety
items.summary: The conclusions state that transformative fire detection research is essential to crew safety on lunar and deep-space missions, and list four priorities.

items.anchor_quote: Fuels prioritized for immediate testing include LIBs and the crew clothing fabric
items.summary: Priority 1: identify realistic fire scenarios and characterise fire signatures of unstudied and understudied fuels; LIBs and the crew clothing fabric to be chosen for Artemis missions are prioritised for immediate testing.
materials: Artemis crew clothing fabric (to be selected)

items.anchor_quote: Proof-of-concept studies in simulated lunar gravity will provide a starting point for lunar habitat experiments
items.summary: Priority 2: evaluate gravity effects on fire signatures and plume transport, starting with proof-of-concept studies in simulated lunar gravity as a basis for lunar habitat experiments.

items.anchor_quote: Emission factors from these studies will enable computational simulations of smoke plume transport
items.summary: Emission factors from those studies would feed computational simulations of smoke plume transport and guide detector placement in future cabins.

items.anchor_quote: Elevated O2 and reduced cabin pressure conditions will influence fire signatures and therefore
items.summary: Priority 3: evaluate exploration-atmosphere effects on fire signatures in reduced gravity; elevated O2 and reduced cabin pressure will influence fire signatures and hence fire detection.

items.anchor_quote: Each variable must be investigated individually in both ground and reduced gravity experiments
items.summary: O2 and pressure must each be investigated separately, in both ground and reduced-gravity experiments.

items.anchor_quote: capable of rapidly identifying smoke components through a combination of different particle and gas
items.summary: Priority 4: develop improved detection systems from spacecraft fire safety data; a transformative system would quickly identify smoke components by combining different particle and gas measurement techniques.

items.anchor_quote: reduce nuisance alarms from suspended cabin and lunar dust
items.summary: Such a combined system would increase the number of detectable fires and cut nuisance alarms caused by suspended cabin dust and lunar dust.
items.scope_notes: Expected benefit, not demonstrated; relates to false (nuisance) alarms, not missed alarms.
